rows.question: When does my maternity leave start if my due date is 15 November 2026?
rows.reply:
In Germany, the period before birth is called Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period). Your employer may not employ you during the last six weeks before the birth, unless you expressly say you are willing to work. You can withdraw that statement at any time for the future.

The six weeks are counted from the expected delivery date shown on a doctor's or midwife's certificate. With an expected date of 15 November 2026, the period before the birth covers the six weeks leading up to that date, so it begins in early October 2026. Use the date on your certificate, not an estimate.

If the baby arrives earlier or later than expected, the period before the birth becomes shorter or longer to match. After the birth, your employer may not employ you for eight weeks. This becomes twelve weeks for premature births and multiple births. It also becomes twelve weeks if a disability is medically diagnosed in the child within the first eight weeks, but only if you apply for this. If the baby comes early, the time lost before the birth is added after it.

You should tell your employer about the pregnancy and the expected delivery date as soon as you know. If your employer asks, you should provide a doctor's or midwife's certificate showing the expected delivery date.

For maternity benefit paid by your statutory health insurance fund before the birth, the fund relies on a doctor's or midwife's certificate stating the expected delivery date.

These protection periods come from the Maternity Protection Act. According to the federal family portal, self-employed women are not covered by it.

rows.question: How long after birth can we apply for Elterngeld without losing money?
rows.reply:
Elterngeld (parental allowance) has to be applied for in writing. The law does not give a fixed application date. It limits back payment instead. Elterngeld is paid retroactively only for the last three months of the child's life before the start of the month of the child's life in which the application is received.

Elterngeld can be received from the day of birth, and it is paid in monthly amounts for months of the child's life. This means an application received more than three months of the child's life after the birth loses the earliest months. Those months are not paid.

The same three-month limit applies if you later change the choices made in your application. Changes are generally not allowed for months that have already been paid, except in cases of particular hardship.

Your Elterngeld office decides the individual application.

rows.question: How much notice do I have to give my employer for Elternzeit?
rows.reply:
For Elternzeit (parental leave (unpaid job-protected leave)), the law sets the notice by the part of the child's life the leave falls in:

- Leave up to the child's third birthday: request it from your employer at least seven weeks before the leave starts.
- Leave between the third birthday and the end of the child's eighth year: request it at least 13 weeks before the leave starts.

The request must be made in text form. The official guidance explains that this includes, for example, an email or a letter without a signature.

When you request leave that falls before the third birthday, you must also state at the same time which periods within two years you will take Elternzeit. If a mother takes Elternzeit directly after her maternity protection period after the birth, that period counts toward these two years.

The law allows a reasonably shorter notice period as an exception where there are urgent reasons. The guidance names premature births as one example and says the period that applies then depends on the individual case. If a mother cannot request leave in time for leave that starts directly after her maternity protection period, for a reason she is not responsible for, she can make the request within one week after that reason ends.

Your employer must give you written confirmation of your Elternzeit. Protection against dismissal starts from the date you request the leave, but no earlier than eight weeks before leave that falls before the third birthday, or 14 weeks before leave that falls after it.

The Familienportal guidance says a different rule applies for children born before 1 July 2015. Under that rule, seven weeks applies to all Elternzeit. The transitional provision behind this is not among the sources here, so I cannot confirm where its boundary lies. If your child was born around that date, check the rule with your employer or the official Elternzeit guidance.

rows.question: How long is maternity protection after the birth if the baby comes early?
rows.reply:
Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) after the birth normally lasts eight weeks. During this time your employer may not employ you.

If the baby comes early, the law gives two separate rules:

1. Any early birth: the period before the birth was shorter than six weeks. The days you lost before the birth are added to the period after the birth. The guidance page puts it this way: the total stays 14 weeks, and the post-birth period ends as many days after eight weeks as the baby arrived before the expected date.

2. Premature birth in the medical sense: the post-birth period is extended from eight to twelve weeks. The days lost before the birth are then added on top of the twelve weeks. The guidance page gives a birth weight under 2,500 grams as one example of a birth that counts medically as premature, and says the total period rises from 14 to 18 weeks.

The same twelve-week rule also applies to twins or more. It also applies when a disability in the child is medically confirmed within eight weeks of the birth, but only if the mother applies for it.

After the birth, you may not waive this period. Pupils and students are an exception: they may resume their studies earlier if they expressly ask to. If an employer asks you to work during Mutterschutz, the guidance page says you can contact your supervisory authority.

rows.question: Can my employer dismiss me while I am pregnant?
rows.reply:
In general, no. From the start of a pregnancy, the law forbids an employer to dismiss a woman. This Kündigungsschutz (protection against dismissal) lasts until the end of the protection period after the birth, and at least until four months after the birth. It also covers the four months after a miscarriage after the twelfth week of pregnancy.

The protection applies if the employer knows about the pregnancy when giving notice, or is told within two weeks of the notice reaching you. Missing the two weeks does no harm if it was not your fault and you inform the employer without delay. The Familienportal adds that the protection also applies if you did not yet know you were pregnant, but you must already have been pregnant when the dismissal reached you.

There is a narrow exception. In special cases that have nothing to do with the pregnancy, the birth or a miscarriage, the highest state authority responsible for occupational safety, or a body it designates, may declare a dismissal permissible. The Familienportal gives examples such as insolvency, partial closure of the business, or a particularly serious breach of duty. The dismissal must then be in writing and must state the reason. Without the authority's approval, the dismissal is invalid.

If you are dismissed without that approval, the Familienportal says you must take the matter to the responsible labour court. It says the claim must normally be filed within 3 weeks of receiving the written dismissal. If no claim is filed, the dismissal is treated as valid. You can file the claim yourself, including orally at the court office, or through a lawyer. The page also advises contacting the supervisory authority. If the authority approved the dismissal, you can challenge that approval separately. That challenge does not replace the court claim.

This explains the general rule only. Whether a particular dismissal is valid is decided by the supervisory authority and the labour court, not by this service.

rows.question: Is there an income limit above which we get no Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes. Under the statute, there is no entitlement to Elterngeld (parental allowance) if the entitled person had zu versteuerndes Einkommen (taxable income) of more than 175,000 euros in the last completed tax assessment period before the child's birth. If another person also meets the entitlement conditions, such as the other parent, the limit applies to both incomes added together: there is no entitlement if their combined zu versteuerndes Einkommen is more than 175,000 euros.

The limit refers to zu versteuerndes Einkommen, not gross income. Gross income is usually considerably higher. Your zu versteuerndes Einkommen is determined by the tax office and shown on your tax assessment. If you have the tax assessment for the calendar year before the birth, it is attached to the Elterngeld application.

You can still apply if your tax assessment is not yet available:
- If your application states that the limit will probably not be exceeded, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation. It can be withdrawn if the limit turns out to have been exceeded.
- If it cannot yet be said whether the limit is exceeded, the decision is provisional until proof is provided.

Older births: the official family portal says different, higher limits applied to some earlier births. The statutory transitional rule for those births is not in the sources available here, so I cannot say which limit applies to a particular birth date.

Which limit applies to your child's birth, and whether your income is above or below it, is decided by the Elterngeld office responsible for your application.

rows.question: How many months of Elterngeld can we get in total?
rows.reply:
The law sets the total as a shared pool of months for both parents, with limits per parent. It does not give one fixed number for every family. Whether your family meets each condition, and how many months you receive, is decided by the authority that handles your Elterngeld (parental allowance) application.

The basic rule:
- Parents together have a claim to 12 monthly payments of basic Elterngeld.
- They get 2 further months, called partner months, if one parent's earnings are reduced in two months of the child's life.
- One parent can receive at most 12 monthly payments of basic Elterngeld.
- A parent only has a claim if they receive Elterngeld for at least two months.

Other ways the total can change:
- Instead of one month of basic Elterngeld, a parent can receive two months of the lower Plus variant.
- Each parent can also receive up to four monthly payments of a partnership bonus. These are set out in a separate section, BEEG §4b, which is not among the sources here. The official family portal describes it as extra months for both parents working part-time at the same time.
- For children born early, the shared basic total rises. It is 13 months if the child was born at least 6 weeks before the expected date, 14 months at 8 weeks, 15 months at 12 weeks and 16 months at 16 weeks. The per-parent maximum rises in the same way.

Time limits and rules that use up months:
- Basic Elterngeld can normally be received only until the child completes the 14th month of life.
- The Plus variant can run until the child completes the 32nd month of life. This only holds while at least one parent receives it in consecutive months from the 15th month onward.
- Months in which a parent receives certain benefits, such as maternity benefits, count as months of basic Elterngeld for that parent.
- Both parents can receive basic Elterngeld at the same time in only one of the first twelve months, except in the cases the law lists. These include multiple births, premature births and certain cases of disability.

rows.question: What is the Partnerschaftsbonus and who qualifies?
rows.reply:
The Partnerschaftsbonus (partnership bonus months) is an extra period of parental allowance for parents who both work part time at the same time. Under the statute, each parent gets one additional monthly payment of the 'Plus' form of parental allowance for each month in which both conditions are met.

Conditions the law sets:
- Both parents work at least 24 and at most 32 hours a week, averaged over the child's month of life. It does not have to be 24 to 32 hours in every single week.
- Both parents meet the general conditions for parental allowance in BEEG §1.
- Both parents take it at the same time, in consecutive months of the child's life.
- Each parent takes it for at least 2 months, and at most 4.

If it later turns out that the hours condition was not met in some of the months applied for, the consecutive-months requirement still counts as met. The official family portal explains that the payment for a month where either parent was outside 24 to 32 hours must be repaid, and both parents lose it for that month. Other months are not affected if the conditions were met in at least 2 months.

Single parents: a parent who parents alone can receive these extra months on their own, if they work 24 to 32 hours a week on average for 2 to 4 consecutive months. This applies in the cases the law lists: the parent meets the tax conditions for single parents and the other parent lives neither with them nor with the child; care by the other parent would endanger the child's welfare; or care by the other parent is impossible, for example because of serious illness or severe disability. rows.question: We forgot to apply for Kindergeld. How far back will they pay?
rows.reply: Kindergeld (child benefit) is paid back for at most the six months before the start of the month in which your application is received. Months earlier than that are not paid out. The law states that the right to Kindergeld itself is not affected by this limit on payment. It is a limit on how far back payment goes, not an application deadline. Each month you wait to apply moves that six-month window forward, so older months drop out of it. The rule also requires that Kindergeld was due to you but was not paid, for example because no application was made. To claim back payment, say in the application that you are applying retroactively and from which date you want Kindergeld. You apply to the family benefits office of your local employment agency. That office decides whether you are entitled and for which months. You can reach the Federal Employment Agency's free service line on 0800 4 555530.

rows.question: How quickly do we have to register the birth at the Standesamt?
rows.reply:
The law says the birth must be reported to the Standesamt (civil registry office) responsible for the place where the child was born, within one week. Parents and other listed persons may report it orally or in writing. Institutions such as hospitals report it in writing.

If your child is born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic, the institution notifies the responsible Standesamt and sends the birth notice. If your child is born at home, the midwife or doctor issues the birth notice, and you must present it to the responsible Standesamt within one week.

One official checklist page says 7 working days. The statute says one week, and the statute is what applies.

If you have not decided on a name yet, the official guidance says you must tell the Standesamt within one month. After that, the Standesamt must inform the family court, which then chooses one parent to decide the name.

The Standesamt in the place of birth handles the registration and can tell you which other documents it needs.

rows.question: Which Standesamt do we go to — the one where we live or where the hospital is?

The Standesamt (civil registry office) for the place where your child is born, not the one where you live. So if the hospital is in a different town from your home, the hospital's town is the one that counts.

For a home birth, you must take that confirmation from the midwife or doctor to the responsible Standesamt within one week yourself.

The portal also says the Standesamt then passes the registration to the residents' registration office automatically. It says the list of other documents you need is on the website of the Standesamt in the town where your child is born.

rows.question: Does my Krankenkasse pay for a midwife?
rows.reply: Yes, statutory health insurance covers midwife care as a general rule. If you are privately insured, the official family portal advises checking with your insurer beforehand which services it covers. Whether a particular service is covered in your case is decided by your Krankenkasse (statutory health insurer).

rows.question: How do we insure the baby after the birth?
rows.reply:
The excerpts describe one route: Familienversicherung (free family cover for dependants) in statutory health insurance. This is the general rule only. Whether your baby is covered this way is decided by the health insurance fund (Krankenkasse).

What the law says. Under SGB V §10, the children of members of a statutory health insurance fund are insured through the member if the child:
- has their residence or usual place of stay in Germany,
- is not insured in their own right,
- is not exempt from compulsory insurance, and
- does not have a regular total income above a set limit.

Children are covered this way up to their 18th birthday. The cover can last longer in certain cases, for example during education or training.

One exception matters for parents. Children are not insured through Familienversicherung if all three of these apply to the parent who is the child's relative:
- they are not a member of a statutory health insurance fund,
- their total income regularly exceeds one twelfth of the annual earnings limit (Jahresarbeitsentgeltgrenze) per month, and
- their income is regularly higher than the member's income.

What to do after the birth. The Familienportal says you must register the birth with the registry office for the place of birth within one week. The registry office issues the birth certificate. The portal lists registering the child with the health insurance fund as one of the things you need the birth certificate for.

Outside our scope. Private health insurance is not covered here. If neither parent is in statutory health insurance, or if the exception above may apply, the excerpts do not say how the child is insured. Ask your health insurance fund or your private insurer.

rows.question: When are the first check-ups for the baby?
rows.reply:
The first check-ups come in the first weeks of your baby's life. The official rule sets a time window for each one, plus a wider tolerance window.

- U1: right after birth. It should be done within the first 30 minutes after the baby is born. If no doctor is present at the birth but a midwife is, the midwife should do it.
- U2: between the 3rd and 10th day of life. The tolerance window is the 3rd to 14th day of life.
- U3: between the 4th and 5th week of life. The tolerance window is the 3rd to 8th week of life.

The next ones are U4 at 3 to 4 months (tolerance 2 to 4½ months), U5 at 6 to 7 months (tolerance 5 to 8 months) and U6 at 10 to 12 months (tolerance 9 to 14 months).

There are ten check-ups in total in the first six years. The rule says each check-up can only be used within its stated period, taking the tolerance window into account. These periods also apply to babies born prematurely. The premature birth is taken into account when the results are assessed.

Children are entitled to these early-detection check-ups until their 18th birthday.

rows.question: What is Mutterschaftsgeld and when do I apply for it?
rows.reply:
Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is money paid for the protection periods before and after the birth, and for the day of birth itself.

Who pays depends on how you are insured:

- If you are a member of a statutory health insurer, the insurer pays Mutterschaftsgeld under the rules of the Fifth Book of the Social Code (SGB V). For women in employment when the protection period before the birth begins, it is based on average net daily earnings over the last three calendar months settled before that period, up to a maximum of 13 euros per calendar day.
- If your average net daily earnings are above 13 euros, your employer pays the difference as a supplement while your employment continues. In certain cases, such as dismissal or employer insolvency, the body responsible for Mutterschaftsgeld pays this supplement instead.
- If you are not a member of a statutory health insurer, Mutterschaftsgeld is paid by the federal government, up to 210 euros in total. The Federal Office for Social Security (Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung) pays it on application.

The protection periods normally begin 6 weeks before the expected due date and end 8 weeks after the birth.

On when to apply: the excerpts I have do not set out an application date or time limit, so I cannot tell you one. What they do say is that for payment before the birth, a certificate from a doctor or midwife stating the expected date of delivery is decisive. For timing and the application itself, ask your statutory health insurer, or the Federal Office for Social Security if you are not statutorily insured.

Mutterschaftsgeld from the statutory health insurer and the employer supplement are counted against Elterngeld for the period from the day of birth. The 210-euro payment from the Federal Office for Social Security is not.

rows.question: We are not married. Is my partner automatically the legal father?
rows.reply:
No. Under federal law, a man is the legal father of a child in only three cases: he is married to the mother at the time of the birth, he has acknowledged paternity, or a court has determined his paternity (BGB §1592). If you are not married when the child is born, your partner becomes the legal father only through a Vaterschaftsanerkennung (acknowledgement of paternity) or a court decision.

How the acknowledgement works:
- It can be made before the child is born (BGB §1594(4)).
- It is voluntary and needs the mother's consent.
- The father must make his declaration in person at a competent office, for example the youth welfare office, a registry office, a local court or a notary. The mother must also give her consent in person. The office records both. Depending on the state, the notary or local court may charge a fee.
- It cannot carry a condition or time limit; one that does is invalid (BGB §1594(3)).
- It is not effective while another man's paternity exists (BGB §1594(2)).
- Its legal effects can generally be relied on only from the moment it becomes effective (BGB §1594(1)).

Parental custody is a separate step. If the parents are not married at the birth, the mother has parental custody from the birth. The Vaterschaftsanerkennung alone does not give the father custody. That also needs declarations by both parents that they want joint custody, a court decision, or the parents marrying after the birth. Your local youth welfare office advises on these questions.

rows.question: How do unmarried parents get joint custody?
rows.reply:
Under federal law, if the parents are not married to each other when the child is born, they have joint parental custody in three cases (BGB §1626a(1)):

1. They both declare that they want to take on custody jointly. Each of these declarations is a Sorgeerklärung (declaration of joint custody).
2. They marry each other.
3. The family court transfers joint custody to them.

If none of these applies, the mother has custody alone (BGB §1626a(3)).

First, paternity must be legally established. The other parent becomes the legal father if he acknowledges the child as his own with the mother's consent, or if a court establishes paternity. Acknowledging paternity does not by itself give the father custody. A Sorgeerklärung or a court decision is still needed.

The declarations can be made, for example, at the youth welfare office or before a notary. They can also be made before the birth.

The court route works like this. One parent applies. The family court transfers joint custody, or part of it, to both parents if this does not conflict with the child's welfare. If the other parent puts forward no reasons against joint custody, and none are otherwise apparent, the law presumes that joint custody does not conflict with the child's welfare (BGB §1626a(2)). The official family portal adds what happens in that case. The court then decides in a simplified procedure. It does not hear the youth welfare office, and it does not hear the parents in person.

Your local youth welfare office gives advice on all questions about parental custody.

rows.question: Will our baby automatically be German if we are both Indian citizens?
rows.reply:
Whether your baby becomes German is decided case by case. I cannot say which way it goes for your family, but I can set out the rule.

Birth to a German parent: a child acquires deutsche Staatsangehörigkeit (citizenship) by birth if one parent is German. This route needs a German parent.

Birth in Germany to foreign parents: a child of foreign parents who is born in Germany acquires deutsche Staatsangehörigkeit through the birth itself if one parent meets both of these conditions:
1. that parent has had their lawful habitual residence in Germany for five years, and
2. that parent holds an unlimited right of residence (or a Swiss residence permit under the EU–Swiss free movement agreement, which does not apply to Indian citizens).
If the conditions are met, the acquisition is entered in the birth register where the child's birth is recorded. Whether the conditions are met for your child is checked when the birth is registered, by the office that keeps that birth register.

If the child does not become German, residence rules apply instead. A child born in Germany is given a residence permit by the authorities on their own initiative if, at the time of birth, both parents hold a residence permit, a settlement permit or an EU long-term residence permit. If only one parent holds one, the permit can be granted. If a parent holds a visa or may stay visa-free at the time of birth, the child's stay counts as permitted until that visa or visa-free stay ends.

The excerpts I have do not cover Indian citizenship law, or whether the child would also hold Indian citizenship. For that, ask the Indian embassy or consulate responsible for where you live in Germany.

rows.question: Does our newborn need a residence permit?
rows.reply:
Whether your child needs a residence permit depends on your family's own status, and only the responsible immigration authority where you live can decide that. Here is what the law says in general.

German citizenship at birth: a child acquires German citizenship at birth if one parent is a German citizen. A child of foreign parents born in Germany also acquires German citizenship if one parent has lawfully had their habitual residence in Germany for five years and holds an unlimited right of residence. A Swiss citizen or their family member may qualify instead with a residence permit under the EU–Swiss free movement agreement. This acquisition is entered in the birth register where the birth is recorded.

Residence permit for a child born in Germany: a child born in Germany may be granted an Aufenthaltserlaubnis (residence permit) by the authority on its own initiative if one parent holds an Aufenthaltserlaubnis, a settlement permit or an EU long-term residence permit. If, at the time of birth, both parents hold one of these permits, the Aufenthaltserlaubnis is granted to the child on the authority's own initiative. The same applies if the parent with sole custody holds one. If a parent holds a visa at the time of birth, or may stay without a visa, the child's stay counts as permitted until that visa or visa-free stay ends.

rows.question: We are getting Mutterschaftsgeld. Does that reduce our Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
The law says that certain maternity benefits are credited against Elterngeld (parental allowance). Under BEEG §3, this covers Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) paid under the statutory health insurance rules and the employer's supplement to Mutterschaftsgeld under MuSchG §20. It applies to the benefits due for the time from the day of the child's birth.

One type is excluded. The Mutterschaftsgeld paid by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung to women who are not members of a statutory health insurer, capped at 210 euros in total (MuSchG §19(2)), is not credited against Elterngeld.

If the maternity benefits are due for only part of a month of the child's life, they are credited only against the matching part of that month's Elterngeld.

The official family portal explains what this means in practice for benefits received for the same child:
- If the maternity benefits are higher than the Elterngeld, only the maternity benefits are paid.
- If the Elterngeld is higher, the difference is paid as Elterngeld on top of the maternity benefits.
- Months in which maternity benefits are due, even for a single day, count as months of basic Elterngeld.

The portal also says the mother's maternity benefits are credited only against the mother's Elterngeld, not against the father's.

Whether and by how much your Elterngeld is affected is decided by the Elterngeld office handling your application. It assesses each case individually.

rows.question: Can I work while receiving Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes, working is possible within limits. The law says a person is entitled to Elterngeld (parental allowance) if, among other conditions, they work not at all or not full-time (BEEG §1(1) no. 4). The statute excerpt does not define the full-time limit. The federal family portal's guidance says you may work up to 32 hours per week while receiving Elterngeld. The portal adds that this describes the rules for children born after August 2021, and that partly different rules apply to children born before 1 September 2021.

Working affects the amount. For months after the birth in which you earn less than you did before the birth, Elterngeld is paid as a percentage of the difference between the two incomes. For this calculation, pre-birth income counts up to at most 2,770 euros (BEEG §2(3)).

If your application says you expect to earn income during the benefit period, the amount is first decided provisionally (BEEG §8(3) no. 3). After the benefit period ends, you must prove your actual earnings for that time (BEEG §8(1)). The portal says the proof for employees is a certificate from your employer about your working hours during the benefit period. Self-employed people give their own statement of their working hours. If your application says you will have no earnings, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation in case you do earn income after all (BEEG §8(2)).

Whether your particular hours and income are within the rules, and how much you would receive, is decided by the Elterngeld office (Elterngeldstelle) responsible for where you live.

rows.question: Where and how do we apply for Kindergeld?
rows.reply:
Where to apply: Kindergeld (child benefit) must be applied for in writing at the responsible Familienkasse. The responsible Familienkasse is the one for the district where the person entitled has their residence. If they have no residence in Germany, it is the one where they habitually stay. If neither applies, it is the one where they work. In all other cases it is Familienkasse Bayern Nord. The Familienkasse receives the application and decides on the claim. The official family portal says that in practice this is usually the Familienkasse of your local Agentur für Arbeit.

Who applies: Kindergeld is paid to only one person per child. If the child lives in the shared household of both parents, the parents decide between themselves which of them is the claimant. If they do not decide, the family court decides on application. Besides the entitled person, anyone with a legitimate interest in the payment may also apply.

How to apply: You can apply electronically or on paper, using the Familienkasse form. The form can be filled in online, then printed and signed. For a newborn child, you can apply fully online with a valid ELSTER certificate, without printing or signing by hand. The application must include your tax identification number and your child's tax identification number.

Documents: For a child under 18, normally only the two tax identification numbers are needed. For a child born abroad or living abroad, submit a copy of the foreign birth certificate or another official document certifying the birth. Supporting documents can be sent online to your Familienkasse. If the Familienkasse asks for further documents, it sets a date for them. If they are not provided by that date, the application can be delayed or refused.

Late applications: According to the family portal, Kindergeld can be paid retroactively for up to 6 months. Months before that are not paid. If you are applying for earlier months, state in the application that you are applying retroactively and from which date.

Questions about applying: the free Bundesagentur für Arbeit service line is 0800 4 555530.

rows.question: What are the Elterngeld rules for a self-employed parent in Bavaria?
rows.reply:
Bavarian procedures, such as which office handles your application and which forms it uses, are outside what this service covers. We cover federal law, Hessen procedures and the Indian consular track. The Elterngeld (parental allowance) rules themselves are federal law, so they apply in Bavaria too. Here is what the federal statute says.

Who can claim: a person who lives or usually stays in Germany, lives in one household with the child, cares for and raises the child themselves, and works not at all or not full time (BEEG §1).

How the amount is set: Elterngeld is 67 percent of income from work before the birth. It is paid up to a maximum of 1,800 euros a month for months with no income from work. The income counted includes positive income from agriculture and forestry, trade or business, and self-employed work, where that income is taxable in Germany. The percentage rises for pre-birth income below 1,000 euros, up to 100 percent, and falls for income above 1,200 euros, down to 65 percent. If you earn less after the birth than before, Elterngeld is that percentage of the difference, and pre-birth income counts up to at most 2,770 euros. The minimum is 300 euros a month (BEEG §2).

Rules that matter for self-employed parents: if your application states expected income from work, you must prove your actual income after the payment period ends. If the tax assessment notice for the last completed tax period before the birth is not yet available, Elterngeld can be paid subject to revocation, or decided provisionally on the information you have credibly shown. A provisional decision also applies if income before the birth cannot be determined, or if you expect to have income from work while receiving Elterngeld (BEEG §8).

How long: Elterngeld comes as a basic monthly amount or as a smaller amount paid over longer, where one basic month can be taken as two months of the longer form. The basic amount can be drawn until the child completes the 14th month of life. One parent can claim at most 12 basic monthly amounts plus up to four partnership bonus amounts, and must claim for at least two months (BEEG §4).

Only the responsible Elterngeld office in Bavaria decides whether you qualify and how much you receive. For Bavarian forms and contacts, ask that office directly.

rows.question: Can you fill in our Elterngeld application form for us?
rows.reply:
We cannot fill in your Elterngeld (parental allowance) application for you. Completing it means making choices about your own case, such as which months to claim, and that belongs to you and the responsible authority. Here is what the law says the application must contain.

The application must be made in writing. It must state for which months of the child's life you claim the basic amount, for which months the Plus variant, and for which months the partnership bonus. (BEEG §7)

The person applying must sign it. The other parent entitled to the benefit must also sign to confirm they have seen it. This does not apply where only one person has custody. The other parent can file their own application at the same time. (BEEG §7)

Payment is made backdated only for the three months of the child's life before the month in which the application is received. Earlier months are not paid. (BEEG §7)

The choices you make in the application can be changed until the end of the payment period. Changes for past months are limited to the last three months. They are not allowed for months already paid, except in cases of special hardship. (BEEG §7)

The official family portal lists the documents usually attached. These are the child's birth certificate and proof of your previous income, for example payslips for the last 12 months. Further documents may be needed depending on the case. (familienportal.de)

The responsible authority is the Elterngeld office designated by your Land for the district where the child lives when you first apply. (BEEG §12) That office can explain the form and decides your application.

rows.question: Based on our situation, will our Elterngeld application be approved?
rows.reply:
We cannot tell you whether your application will be approved. Only the authority that handles your claim decides that, and that is your Elterngeld office. Here is what the law says in general.

Who can get Elterngeld (parental allowance): the law gives the right to a person who (1) has a residence or habitual abode in Germany, (2) lives in one household with the child, (3) cares for and raises the child themselves, and (4) does not work, or does not work full time. For multiple births there is only one claim. The law also names further groups who can claim in certain cases, for example some people posted abroad, people who have taken in a child with the aim of adoption, or relatives up to the third degree if the parents cannot care for the child because of serious illness, severe disability or death.

How to apply: Elterngeld must be applied for in writing. It is paid retroactively only for the last three months of the child's life before the month in which the application is received. Earlier months are not paid. In the application you state which months you are claiming Basiselterngeld, Elterngeld Plus or the partnership bonus for.

If you disagree with the decision: you can only have it reviewed by lodging a written objection with your Elterngeld office within one month of receiving the decision. Lawsuits against the decision go to the social courts.

Whether these conditions are met in your case, and how much is paid, is decided by your Elterngeld office.

rows.question: How much tax will we save if I switch to Steuerklasse 3 before the birth?
rows.reply:
We cannot tell you how much tax you would save by changing tax class. That is a calculation for your household, and tax-class choices and their tax effects belong to the tax office or a tax adviser. The excerpts we have do not describe tax savings at all. They only describe how your tax class is used when parental allowance is calculated.

What the law says about tax class and parental allowance:

- Income tax is deducted using your tax class and, where one applies, the factor under § 39f of the Income Tax Act. Tax class VI is not taken into account. If you had no tax class in the assessment period, for example because you are self-employed, tax class IV without a factor is used.
- If you changed tax class before the birth, the newest tax class is used for the simplified net-income calculation. The older one is used only if it applied for longer within the whole assessment period. The same applies to other deduction details, such as the number of child allowances.
- If you work after the birth, the same deduction details as before the birth are used. Changing tax class again after the birth has no further effect on parental allowance.

Whether and how a change of tax class affects your own parental allowance is decided by the parental allowance office when it assesses your application. For the tax effect of switching, ask the tax office or a tax adviser.
